# Award-winning study puts AI's impact on radiology into perspective 

AI could reduce radiologists’ workload by one-third. So why does the need for radiologists keep growing?

That’s the question Curtis Langlotz, MD, PhD, professor of radiology, medicine and biomedical data science, explored in his paper, The Effect of AI on the Radiologist Workforce: A Task-Based Analysis, which was awarded Scientific Paper of the Year in the 2026 Minnies, AuntMinnie.com’s event recognizing excellence in radiology. 

The question a decade in the making

In 2016, predictions about how artificial intelligence (AI) would impact radiology were mainly negative. One prominent voice, Geoffrey Hinton, famously suggested that medical students should stop training in radiology altogether because within five years, AI will be better than radiologists. 

Dr. Langlotz worried about the message that these words would send to radiologists of all seniority levels. 

Curtis Langlotz, MD, PhD

He responded with an editorial arguing that AI was unlikely to make radiologists obsolete. Nearly a decade later, he says, that argument has largely held up. AI has not replaced radiologists in any material way, but questions still remain about how the technology will affect the profession.

But it wasn’t until 2024 that the idea for the study took shape, when Dr. Langlotz was invited to speak at an international meeting on AI and the radiology workforce. Rather than revisit the broad question of whether AI will replace radiologists, he wanted to update his earlier arguments with what he calls “the best version of the truth” about AI’s potential effects, making the case as quantitative and evidence based as possible.

To do that, he broke radiology into individual tasks, including interpreting images, selecting imaging protocols, communicating with referring clinicians and drafting reports. He then evaluated 15 categories of AI applications that could affect those tasks, using published research and other available evidence to estimate their potential impact over five years.

His results suggest that gains in efficiency from AI do not necessarily mean fewer radiologists will be needed. As imaging volumes continue to rise, AI may change how radiologists work without reducing demand for their expertise.

What the numbers reveal about AI’s potential impact

The study projects that AI could reduce the hours of radiologist work required by 33%, with estimates ranging from 14% to 49%. Two applications account for much of the projected change: 1) automated report drafting, which could shorten the time needed to produce imaging reports, and 2) study delegation, which could allow AI to identify certain studies that may not require a radiologist’s interpretation.

The impact on these applications is also not expected to be the same across all areas of radiology. Automated report drafting could affect a broad range of imaging exams, while study delegation could have a particularly substantial effect in radiography and mammography. Other applications, including image triage and automated detection of abnormalities, could also change how radiologists review studies, though their projected effects on time are more modest.

More efficient work does not necessarily mean less demand

The distinction between reducing the time needed for a task and reducing the need for radiologists is important. Imaging volumes have continued to grow, with cross-sectional imaging studies nearly doubling over the past decade, while the radiologist workforce has remained relatively stable. Dr. Langlotz argues that continued growth in demand for imaging could absorb much of the productivity gained through AI.

In this scenario, AI would take on some of the repetitive or time-consuming parts of radiology, allowing radiologists to focus their time elsewhere. The profession would change, but the need for radiologists would remain.

Enlarging the evidence base

Dr. Langlotz is now working with a radiology resident and computer science graduate students with medical training to build on the analysis. The team is conducting a formal literature review of AI’s effects on individual radiology tasks and assembling an expert panel to develop estimates where published evidence is limited. They plan to use those findings in a more formal meta-analysis and sensitivity analysis.

Dr. Langlotz also directs Stanford’s Center for Artificial Intelligence in Medicine and Imaging (AIMI), an interdisciplinary center established in 2018 to advance the development, evaluation and responsible use of AI in health care. The center brings together clinicians, computer scientists, engineers, statisticians and other researchers to develop AI methods for medical challenges and make data and tools more widely accessible.
